**The Weight of a Single Word**

There’s a moment, just before dawn, when the world holds its breath. The air is thick with the kind of silence that isn’t absence but presence—an almost tangible thing, like the hum of a tuning fork just before the orchestra begins. I’ve always loved that moment. It’s the only time I feel like I’m not just *in* the world, but *part* of it, a single thread in some vast, unraveling tapestry.

Words have always been my way of stitching myself into that tapestry. Not the grand, sweeping declarations—the ones that echo in marble halls or crackle through speakers at rallies—but the small, quiet ones. The ones that slip between the cracks of everyday life like weeds pushing through pavement. *"I’m here."* *"I see you."* *"This too shall pass."* Simple, but heavy. A single word can be a lifeline or a blade.

I think about the first time I realized this. I was twelve, sitting in the back of my grandmother’s car, watching the highway blur past the window. She was humming along to some old song on the radio, her fingers tapping the steering wheel in time. Then, without warning, she turned down the volume and said, *"You’re going to be okay."*

Four words. That’s all. But they landed in my chest like a stone dropped into still water, sending ripples outward until my whole body felt the weight of them. Not because they were profound—though they were—but because they were *true*. Or at least, they felt true in that moment. And sometimes, that’s enough.

---

Language is a strange thing. It’s the tool we use to build bridges, but it’s also the thing that keeps us apart. We say *"I love you"* and mean a thousand different things. We say *"I’m fine"* and mean *"I am drowning."* We say *"It’s complicated"* when what we really mean is *"I don’t know how to explain this without breaking something."*

I’ve spent years collecting words like some people collect coins or seashells. Not just the pretty ones—the sharp ones, too. The ones that cut. *"Betrayal."* *"Loneliness."* *"Regret."* I hoard them in the back of my mind, turning them over like artifacts, wondering what they mean, where they came from, how they got so heavy. Maybe it’s because I’m afraid that if I don’t hold onto them, they’ll disappear. Or maybe it’s because I’m afraid they *won’t*.

There’s a story I read once about a man who could see the weight of words. Not their meaning, not their sound, but their *mass*—how much they pressed down on the people who carried them. He said *"sorry"* was the heaviest of all, because it was never just an apology. It was a confession, a plea, a white flag. It was the sound of someone trying to unbreak what could never be unbroken.

I think about that a lot. About the words we swallow because they’re too heavy to speak. About the ones we spit out like poison, only to realize too late that they’ve already done their damage. About the ones we never get to say at all.

---

I had a friend once who only spoke in questions. Not because he was unsure, but because he believed answers were traps. *"What if we’re all just stories we tell ourselves?"* he’d ask over coffee, stirring his cup like he was trying to dissolve the sugar into the universe. *"What if the only thing that’s real is the space between the words?"*

I never knew how to answer him. Maybe because I was afraid he was right.

There’s a kind of magic in not knowing. In sitting with the silence, in letting the question hang in the air like smoke. But there’s also a kind of terror. Because words are how we make sense of things. They’re how we name our monsters, how we build our shelters, how we say *"I was here"* before we disappear.

I wonder if that’s why we’re so afraid of the unsaid. Why we fill the quiet with noise, why we’d rather lie than admit we don’t know. Because if we stop talking, even for a second, we might hear the truth: that all our words are just echoes. That we’re all just trying to outrun the silence.

---

I’ve been thinking a lot about time lately. Not in the grand, philosophical sense—though I’ve done my share of that—but in the small, practical ways. How it stretches and snaps like taffy. How a single hour can feel like a lifetime, and a lifetime can slip by in the blink of an eye. How the past is always closer than it seems, and the future is always just out of reach.

They say time heals all wounds, but I don’t think that’s true. I think time just teaches us how to carry them. How to fold them up small enough to fit in our pockets, how to pull them out when we need to remember why we’re still here.

I’ve carried a lot of words with me over the years. Some I’ve let go of. Others I’ve held onto so tightly they’ve left marks. But the ones that stay with me the longest aren’t the ones that were said to me. They’re the ones I never got to say.

*"I forgive you."* *"I was wrong."* *"Don’t go."*

Maybe that’s the real weight of words—not in the speaking, but in the not-speaking. In the things we leave unsaid until it’s too late.

---

I don’t know how to end this. I don’t know how to tie it all up neatly, to give it a shape that makes sense. Maybe because life doesn’t work that way. Maybe because words don’t either.

But I do know this: if you’re reading this, you’re still here. And that means you still have time. Time to say the things you’ve been holding back. Time to listen to the things you’ve been ignoring. Time to let the silence in, just for a little while, and see what it has to tell you.

So here’s my word for you, the one I’m offering like a coin pressed into your palm:

*Breathe.*

That’s all. Just breathe. The rest will come. Or it won’t. But either way, you’ll still be here. And that’s enough.
